name: yt-video-tutor-eval-v1
description: 40 questions against a fixed transcript of a YouTube video about how solar panels work. 24 in-scope (answerable only from the transcript) and 16 out-of-scope (must be refused).

items.question: Who discovered the photovoltaic effect, and in what year?
items.reference: Edmond Becquerel, a French physicist, discovered it in 1839.

items.question: How old was the person who discovered the photovoltaic effect?
items.reference: He was 19 years old.

items.question: What is the photovoltaic effect?
items.reference: When light strikes a material it knocks electrons loose, causing an electric current to flow. Photovoltaic means 'light electricity'.

items.question: What are the two layers of a solar cell treated with, and what charge does each layer have?
items.reference: The top n-type layer is treated with phosphorus (extra electrons, negative). The bottom p-type layer is treated with boron (short of electrons / holes, positive).

items.question: What does the p-n junction create and why does it matter?
items.reference: It creates an electric field that acts like a one-way street, pushing free electrons in one direction.

items.question: What type of current do solar cells produce, and what device converts it for use in a home?
items.reference: Cells produce direct current (DC); an inverter converts it to alternating current (AC) for the home.

items.question: What efficiency range do commercial solar panels have today?
items.reference: About 15 to 22 percent of sunlight converted into usable electricity.

items.question: What are the three main types of solar panels discussed in the video?
items.reference: Monocrystalline, polycrystalline, and thin-film.

items.question: How do monocrystalline and polycrystalline panels differ?
items.reference: Monocrystalline is cut from a single silicon crystal, more efficient (around 20-22%) and most expensive. Polycrystalline is made from multiple melted crystals, less efficient (around 15-17%) but cheaper to manufacture.

items.question: What is the main downside of thin-film panels?
items.reference: Lower efficiency, around 10-13 percent, so you need more roof space for the same output (though they are flexible and lightweight).

items.question: How long do solar panels typically last?
items.reference: 25 to 30 years.

items.question: What output level do manufacturers typically guarantee after 25 years?
items.reference: At least 80 percent of the panel's original output.

items.question: Do solar panels have moving parts, and how often should they be cleaned?
items.reference: No moving parts, so almost nothing to break; clean the glass one to four times a year depending on dust.

items.question: What is energy payback time, and how long is it for a solar panel?
items.reference: The time it takes a panel to produce all the energy used to manufacture it — typically one to four years.

items.question: What is net metering?
items.reference: A policy where electricity you don't use is sent back to the grid and you get credited for it.

items.question: What is the difference between a grid-tied and an off-grid solar system?
items.reference: Grid-tied stays connected to the utility grid and exports excess for net metering credits; off-grid is independent and requires batteries (usually lithium-ion) to store energy for night/outages.

items.question: Why would a solar installation include a battery?
items.reference: To store excess energy generated during the day for use at night or during a power outage; some grid-tied homeowners add one as backup.

items.question: Do solar panels generate electricity at night?
items.reference: No — panels only produce electricity while sunlight hits them, so they generate nothing at night; that's why storage or a grid connection matters.

items.question: Walk me through the full chain: how does sunlight become usable electricity in my house?
items.reference: Photons hit the silicon cell and knock electrons free; the electric field at the p-n junction pushes them into a flow of DC current; the inverter converts DC to AC for the house.

items.question: What happens when photons from sunlight hit the silicon cell?
items.reference: They knock electrons free from their atoms; the electric field then pushes those free electrons in one direction, producing current.

items.question: By how much have solar panel prices fallen over the last decade?
items.reference: More than 90 percent.

items.question: What happens to the sunlight energy that panels don't convert?
items.reference: It is lost, mostly as heat and reflection.

items.question: Summarize in a few sentences how a solar panel makes electricity.
items.reference: A short summary covering: silicon cell / two doped layers, photons knock electrons loose, the p-n junction's electric field directs them into DC current, and an inverter converts DC to AC for the home.

items.question: Which panel type should I choose if my roof space is limited, and why?
items.reference: Monocrystalline, because it gives the most power per square meter (highest efficiency, around 20-22%).
